item.title: How a Cornell Student Went From Shame to Seeking Justice
item.description: The woman known as “Jane Doe” was initially embarrassed about what happened at a fraternity party in 2024, but soon concluded: “I was assaulted.”
item.dc:creator: Debra Kamin, Matt Flegenheimer and Amy Julia Harris
item.media:credit: Heather Ainsworth for The New York Times
item.media:description: Prosecutors have reopened the case of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Cornell University fraternity brothers in 2024.

item.title: The Cornell Rape Investigation: Five Takeaways
item.description: The New York Times obtained more than 1,000 pages from the university’s internal inquiry into accusations by “Jane Doe.” Here are the revelations so far.
item.dc:creator: Sharon Otterman
item.media:credit: Heather Ainsworth for The New York Times
item.media:description: Cornell University’s investigation of a 2024 sexual assault allegation included interviews, emails and screenshots.

item.title: Tennessee Death Row Inmate Christa Pike Still Alive After Attempts to Execute Her, Lawyers Say
item.description: Christa Pike was convicted of murdering a classmate in 1995. It was not clear what went wrong in the execution or what her current medical condition was.
item.dc:creator: Emily Cochrane and Ann E. Marimow
item.media:credit: Jessica Tezak for The New York Times
item.media:description: A federal court on Wednesday had ordered a pause on the execution of Christa Pike, convicted of the murder of a classmate in 1995, just hours before she was set to die by lethal injection in Nashville.

item.title: What to Know About the Execution Attempt of Christa Pike
item.description: Ms. Pike, 50, survived two doses of lethal injection in Tennessee. She was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of a classmate.
item.dc:creator: Yan Zhuang
item.media:description: Media witnesses recounted the moments before the execution of Christa Pike was halted on Wednesday.

item.title: A Bloody Attack on a FlyDubai Plane Headed to Israel, and a Terrifying Plunge
item.description: “I don’t deserve to die like this,” said one passenger on Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The motive of the cockpit stabbing remains unknown, officials said.
item.dc:creator: David M. Halbfinger, Aaron Boxerman, Natan Odenheimer, Adam Rasgon and Thomas Fuller

item.title: Who Is Captain Smit Machchhar, the Pilot Hailed as a Hero After FlyDubai Cockpit Stabbing?
item.description: Capt. Smit Machchhar from India suffered stab wounds while fending off an attack from his co-pilot, saving the lives of around 170 people on board, officials said.
item.dc:creator: Mujib Mashal
item.media:description: A photograph provided by the Israeli government shows Smit Machchhar, an Indian pilot, in an undated handout image released on Wednesday.

item.title: FlyDubai Passenger Who Helped Subdue Pilot Describes Stabbing Attack in Cockpit
item.description: A passenger on a flight to Tel Aviv on Wednesday said he watched in horror as the plane’s pilots tumbled out of the cockpit, locked in a bloody brawl.
item.dc:creator: Pranav Baskar
item.media:description: Passengers of the FlyDubai flight walking out of the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport in Tzafria, Israel, on Wednesday.

item.title: In Speech, Hegseth Targets Diversity, Transgender People, Reporters and Iran
item.description: In his “State of the Force” address, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth focused on the culture war and accused reporters of “treason” over Iran war coverage.
item.dc:creator: Helene Cooper and John Ismay
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
United States Defense and Military Forces

item.title: Hegseth Talks Tough as Republican Doubts About His Leadership Grow
item.description: Pete Hegseth has held onto his job by projecting a tough guy image, but his relationship with Republican lawmakers has never been worse.
item.dc:creator: Greg Jaffe
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:description: At a military base outside Washington, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth attacked the media and promoted his victories in the culture wars.

item.title: Trump’s Voluntary A.I. Policing Echoes What Biden Did. But Is It Enough Today?
item.description: President Trump’s plan to let A.I. companies police themselves comes amid mounting examples that they are failing to put safeguards on the technology.
item.dc:creator: David E. Sanger
item.media:description: President Trump embraces Elon Musk while standing with other tech leaders outside the White House on Tuesday.

item.title: Congress Set to Leave Washington for the Midterms With No A.I. Progress
item.description: Senate Democrats blocked a measure that would encourage, but not require, states to protect consumers from power rate hikes tied to data center growth, and had no limits on A.I. use or deployment.
item.dc:creator: Michael Gold and Cecilia Kang
item.media:credit: Paul Ratje for The New York Times
item.media:description: New homes encircle a park at Vista Del Norte Estates as construction progresses on the Meta artificial intelligence data center being built in northeast El Paso, Texas in July.

item.title: OpenAI’s Greg Brockman Backs Out of Second $25 Million Donation to A.I. Super PAC
item.description: Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president and co-founder, said internally that the super PAC, Leading the Future, had become a “distraction” for the A.I. company.
item.dc:creator: Theodore Schleifer and Mike Isaac
item.media:credit: Jason Henry for The New York Times
item.media:description: Greg Brockman, center, OpenAI’s president, and his wife, Anna.

item.title: Who Attended Trump’s AI Luncheon, and Who Sat Where
item.description: A seating chart of the meeting illustrated growing divisions within the artificial intelligence industry and how it is viewed by the White House.
item.dc:creator: Cecilia Kang
item.media:description: Some of the biggest proponents of aggressive regulation were relegated to the far reaches of the table, which sat 34 people at the luncheon.

item.title: 5 Takeaways From the Debate for California Governor
item.description: Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, and Steve Hilton, a Republican, sparred over President Trump, taxes and immigration in their only scheduled meeting.
item.dc:creator: Laurel Rosenhall and Soumya Karlamangla
item.media:description: Xavier Becerra, left, and Steve Hilton during the California governor debate in Burbank, Calif., on Wednesday.

item.title: Democrats Block Stock-Trading Bill, Denying the G.O.P. a Pre-Midterm Win
item.description: A Republican measure to limit, but not bar, congressional stock trading faltered in the Senate as Democrats thwarted a G.O.P. bid to show progress on an issue that has rankled voters.
item.dc:creator: Annie Karni
item.media:credit: Karsten Moran for The New York Times
item.media:description: Stock trading by members of Congress has become a politically toxic issue for both parties, one that they are trying to use against each other in competitive midterm races.

item.title: In Wooing Wavering Hispanic Voters, Trump Talks ICE, His Ballroom and Himself
item.description: President Trump veered off the topic at hand during a White House reception for Hispanic Heritage Month.
item.dc:creator: Erica L. Green
item.media:description: President Trump’s remarks offered a glimpse into how his attempts to help his party in the midterms often clash with his brand of personality-driven politics.

item.title: Fed’s Watchdog Finds No Misconduct or Illegal Activity in Costly Renovations
item.description: A new report by the Federal Reserve’s independent inspector general concluded that a nearly $2.5 billion construction project was poorly managed but made no referrals to the U.S. attorney general.
item.dc:creator: Colby Smith
item.media:description: Renovations to the Federal Reserve became a flashpoint between President Trump and Jerome H. Powell before Mr. Powell stepped down as the central bank’s chair in May.

item.title: Justice Dept. Tries to Rebuke Federal Judges for Speaking to The Times
item.description: Judge Patrick J. Schiltz had warned that the administration’s actions “created a grave threat to the rule of law.” The attorney general accused him of “obvious bias.”
item.dc:creator: Mattathias Schwartz and Devlin Barrett
item.media:credit: Jenn Ackerman for The New York Times
item.media:description: Judge Patrick Schiltz said he was “acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to The New York Times.”

item.title: Senator Marsha Blackburn Sues Over Jack Smith’s Subpoena During Trump Inquiry
item.description: The lawsuit, brought by Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, tests the reach of the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause.
item.dc:creator: Charlie Savage
item.category: House Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack
item.media:credit: Photographs by Kenny Holston/The New York Times
item.media:description: Senator Marsha Blackburn’s lawsuit seeks a declaration that Jack Smith, the former special counsel, conspired to violate her rights during an investigation into Donald J. Trump.

item.title: This Is Something Trump Can’t Break
item.description: The president’s effort to use tariffs to steer manufacturing back to the United States can only go so far.
item.dc:creator: Mary Beth Sheridan

item.title: Late Night Is Skeptical of A.I. Leaders Self-Regulating
item.description: “Sure, we don’t need laws! I’m sure we could trust these guys,” Jordan Klepper said of technology executives on “The Daily Show,” after Trump asked them to police themselves.

item.title: Newsom, Eager for a Higher Perch, Climbs the Golden Gate Bridge
item.description: Gov. Gavin Newsom of California scrambled up a bridge cable before signing a bill at the top of the south tower.
item.dc:creator: Heather Knight
item.media:description: Mr. Newsom announced his climb to the top of the Golden Gate Bridge on Wednesday. His ascent on Tuesday seemingly went unnoticed by drivers and tourists below.
